## 1. Reporting transparency > Reporting guidelines
Source: The Magenta Book: central government guidance on evaluation (`magenta-book`), HM Treasury. Authority: mandatory. page last updated 2026-05-15.
Cite inline as: ([The Magenta Book: central government guidance on evaluation: Reporting guidelines](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/transparency-in-government-evaluation-research-t-i-g-e-r-html#reporting-guidelines))

Section text (verbatim):
> Reporting guidelines outline a structured approach to writing evaluation reports so they provide a clear and complete account of how an evaluation was conducted. These guidelines provide detailed recommendations on how to describe the intervention of interest, the methodological approach employed, the construction of treatment and control groups, the outcomes used in the analysis, data collection instruments, missing data, statistical methods and research ethics. These checklists help evaluators to report their evaluations completely and transparently, ensuring readers have the information they need to critically appraise, interpret and use the research.

## 2. Chapter 9: Tailoring and embedding The Teal Book in an organisation > 9.4 Considerations for organisational tailoring and adopting > 9.4.6 Developing tailoring guidelines
Source: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government (`teal-book`), Government Project Delivery. Authority: advisory. text last seen to change 2026-10-15 (re-read weekly from the publisher's daily PDF).
Cite inline as: ([The Teal Book: Project delivery in government: 9.4.6 Developing tailoring guidelines](https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-b-tailoring-and-adopting/chapter-9-tailoring-and-embedding-the-teal-book-in-an-organisation/#:~:text=9.4.6%20Developing%20tailoring%20guidelines,-When%20developing%20the))

Section text (verbatim):
> When developing the project delivery framework, it is helpful to agree rules on what can be tailored, who can tailor it, and who can provide advice, guidance and approvals.
> The goal is always to keep project delivery proportionate to the scale and complexity of the work being undertaken and so basing tailoring rules on these 2 factors can be helpful, using the Risk potential assessment form as a starting point.

## 3. Further resources > Guidelines for AI Procurement
Source: Data and AI Ethics Framework (`data-ethics`), Central Digital and Data Office. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2025-12-18.
Cite inline as: ([Data and AI Ethics Framework: Guidelines for AI Procurement](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#guidelines-for-ai-procurement))

Section text (verbatim):
> Use these guidelines when procuring AI-powered solutions.

## 4. Reporting transparency > Reporting guidelines > Box 6: Reporting guidelines: Ministry of Justice, Justice Data Lab
Source: The Magenta Book: central government guidance on evaluation (`magenta-book`), HM Treasury. Authority: mandatory. page last updated 2026-05-15.
Cite inline as: ([The Magenta Book: central government guidance on evaluation: Box 6: Reporting guidelines: Ministry of Justice, Justice Data Lab](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/transparency-in-government-evaluation-research-t-i-g-e-r-html#box-6))

Section text (verbatim):
> The Ministry of Justice’s Justice Data Lab uses a standardised reporting template to report on the results of all the interventions that it evaluates. This template provides clear information on the intervention of interest, a description of treatment and control groups, information on the outcome variables, and a comprehensive reporting of the results of the analysis.
> The template also provides a consistent approach to describing effect sizes and uncertainty estimates, making it easier to compare the effects of different interventions. For example, effects are presented in terms of the number of people reoffending per 100 prisoners. Effect sizes are described so that they are understandable for a lay audience, and in numerical and visual form.
> The template also includes a clear statement about what can – and what cannot – be inferred from a given analysis. This includes exemplar text on ‘What you can say about the one-year reoffending rate’; and ‘What you cannot say about the one-year reoffending rate’ on the basis of the results presented in the evaluation report.

## 5. Chapter 27: Communications > 27.6 How to manage communications > 27.6.1 What to consider when communicating > 27.6.1.2 Ensuring compliance with the government identity and brand
Source: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government (`teal-book`), Government Project Delivery. Authority: advisory. text last seen to change 2026-10-15 (re-read weekly from the publisher's daily PDF).
Cite inline as: ([The Teal Book: Project delivery in government: 27.6.1.2 Ensuring compliance with the government identity and brand](https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-27-communications/#:~:text=27.6.1.2%20Ensuring%20compliance%20with%20the%20government%20identity%20and%20brand,-The%20Government%20Functional))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "For those engaged in project delivery, this normally means that communications should follow the brand of the organisation they are a part of or are delivering for."
- [RECOMMENDED] "When considering how to brand communications, project delivery professionals should refer to the HM Government brand guidelines, the organisation’s brand guidelines and, where appropriate, consult with relevant communications teams in the organisation or Cabinet Office."

Section text (verbatim):
> The Government Functional Standard for Communication requires government departments, agencies and arm’s length bodies comply with the HM Government identity guidelines.
> The unifying element of the government’s identity is the Royal Coat of Arms, which only departments of HM Government and its organisations are permitted to use, other than agreed exceptions for individual departments, in Scotland (where the Royal Arms of Scotland is used) and overseas.
> For those engaged in project delivery, this normally means that communications should follow the brand of the organisation they are a part of or are delivering for. For larger-scale work, a separate brand might be needed, especially where the public are impacted and need to be communicated with, or where the organisation’s brand for communications is not appropriate. When considering how to brand communications, project delivery professionals should refer to the HM Government brand guidelines, the organisation’s brand guidelines and, where appropriate, consult with relevant communications teams in the organisation or Cabinet Office.
> See Government Communication Service’s SAFER framework for digital brand safety for guidance on ensuring digital brand safety when placing paid advertising and organic content across online platforms.
